extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and students concerned with the logic of induction and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for assessing the validity, scope, and certainty of inductive generalizations and for distinguishing different kinds of uniformities (succession/causation vs co-existence/properties of kinds). Useful for evaluating scientific claims and the reasoning that supports them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of universality of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive methods presuppose the universality of the law of causation — that every event has some antecedent cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that this universality is an assumption built into many inductive procedures; it must not be taken for granted as evidence. The argument that a particular antecedent must be the cause often relies on assuming that an effect must have some cause at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief vs evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A disposition to believe (even if ubiquitous or instinctive) is not itself proof of an external fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute psychological certainty or instinctive belief for objective evidence. Evidence should be what the judging faculty ought to yield to — faculties of sense and consciousness — not merely what induces belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of simple enumeration (induction per enumerationem simplicem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization from mere absence of known counter-instances (simple enumeration) is a common, early form of induction but is fallible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such generalizations as providing provisional assurance; they can be useful for ordinary conduct but are precarious for establishing universal laws. Improve them by testing against stronger inferences or broader experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement by substituting less fallible forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific induction seeks to replace more fallible inductive forms with operations grounded on the same process in less fallible ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, use methods (e.g., the Four Methods of Induction) that reduce fallibility compared with crude enumeration. The goal is to correct inartificial generalizations by relating them to broader, more secure inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmability by subsequent experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode of concluding from experience is untrustworthy if later experience refuses to confirm it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer conclusions that remain consistent under further observation; generalizations should be judged by whether subsequent experience corroborates them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of trustworthiness vs generalization size
rubrics_metrics.description: The precariousness of simple enumeration is inversely proportional to the largeness of the generalization: broader claims from simple enumeration are more likely to be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially skeptical of wide-ranging universal claims derived from limited enumeration; narrow, well-observed domains yield more reliable generalizations from simple enumeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical law within limits (probability vs universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fact observed repeatedly and never found false may be affirmed as an empirical law true within certain limits of time, place, and circumstance if coincidences exceed what chance would produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a generalization is an empirical law, consider whether the number of confirming instances is greater than expected by chance and specify the temporal, spatial, and circumstantial limits of its validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving certainty from the law of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of causation, once established, can impart greater certainty to subordinate inductive propositions when they are deduced from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer showing that a narrower generalization follows from, or is consistent with, the universal law of causation; such linkage increases the degree of assurance beyond that provided by crude enumeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing generalizations by stronger inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: To test a generalization, show that it either follows from, or conflicts with, some stronger induction resting on a broader foundation of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stronger, more comprehensive inductions as the standard against which to test and correct weaker generalizations; this is characterized as the beginning and end of the logic of induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for collocations and counteracting agencies before extending scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not extend an empirical generalization beyond observed limits without excluding that its truth is due to special collocations or to the accidental absence of counteracting agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extending a generalization to wider regions or times, seek evidence that the same collocations and absence/presence of counteracting causes hold; otherwise restrict the claim to the domain where these conditions have been observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between uniformities of succession and of co-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities of succession (temporal sequences) fall under causation; uniformities of co-existence concern simultaneous properties and may not depend on causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply different investigative logic to succession (where elimination methods apply) versus co-existence (where such methods often fail). Do not conflate the two when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate vs derivative properties in co-existence claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-existences among ultimate properties (properties of Kinds) differ from co-existences among derivative properties (effects); whether properties are ultimate determines how to treat the generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a property is an ultimate feature of a Kind or a consequence of causal conditions. If derivative, treat the co-existence as an empirical law amenable to inductive testing; if ultimate, recognize it as a claim about the Kind with no analogous elimination principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a general axiom for co-existences
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general axiom for uniformities of co-existence analogous to the law of causation for succession; thus rigorous scientific induction (elimination, agreement/difference, concomitant variations) is often inapplicable to co-existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about claiming universal co-existence (e.g., 'All crows are black'); the methods that work for causation do not straightforwardly apply to properties of Kinds, so such claims lack the same foundation of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying elimination method to properties-of-kind inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon erred in applying the principle of elimination (searching for an invariable co-existent 'form') to co-existences; objects rarely share circumstances beyond the property in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on elimination or the search for a common accompanying circumstance when attempting to determine whether a property is universally co-existent with a Kind; such inquiries usually fail to yield results.
